input: This worked example determines the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min, starting from a measured rate constant. The rate constant $k$ was measured as 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min. For a first-order reaction, the rate constant $k$ (min-1) is connected to the half-life $t_{1/2}$ (min) by the relation $t_{1/2} = \ln(2)/k$, and the fraction remaining after a time $t$ (min) is given by $\exp(-k t)$. The half-life $t_{1/2}$ can be understood as the time needed for the concentration to drop to one half of its initial value, while the fraction remaining expresses the concentration at time $t$ as a proportion of the initial concentration. Substituting $k$ = 0.069 min-1 into the half-life relation gives $t_{1/2}$ = 10 min. Substituting the same value of $k$ = 0.069 min-1, together with $t$ = 60 min, into the decay relation gives a fraction remaining of 0.02. This can be cross-checked very simply: 60 min is equivalent to six half-lives of 10 min each, and halving the concentration six times over leaves only a small residue, broadly consistent with a remaining fraction of 0.02. It is worth emphasising that the half-life of 10 min and the fraction remaining of 0.02 are tied to the temperature at which the rate constant was measured, since a different temperature would produce a different rate constant and hence different results. Finally, it should be noted that both of these relations hold only for a first-order reaction; a reaction of any other order follows a completely different decay law, and the approach used here would not be applicable to it.

The half-life $t_{1/2}$ is the time at which the concentration has fallen to one half of its initial value, and the fraction remaining is the concentration at time $t$ divided by the initial concentration. The initial concentration appears in neither relation, which is why the half-life of a first-order reaction does not depend on the starting concentration. Substitution of $k$ = 0.069 min-1 in the half-life relation gives $t_{1/2}$ = 10 min. Substitution of $k$ = 0.069 min-1 and $t$ = 60 min in the decay relation gives the fraction remaining as 0.02.
